a: the third year of King Belshazzar's rule
p: About 550 BC on the sixth-century reading; the Babylonian records never number his years as king.
b: Belshazzar was the son of Nabonidus, the last Babylonian king. The Nabonidus Chronicle and the Verse Account of Nabonidus show Nabonidus living away at Teima in Arabia for years while his son managed affairs in Babylon, and this is the setting the book assumes (compare Daniel 5:7, 16, 29, where Belshazzar offers 'third ruler in the kingdom'). The vision therefore falls near 550 BC, before Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC. Defenders of a sixth-century date point to the accuracy of the title; critical scholars (Collins) answer that the author could have drawn it from Jewish memory or tradition, and note that the book makes Belshazzar a king and the son of Nebuchadnezzar. The vision comes after Daniel 7, which is dated to Belshazzar's first year (7:1).

p: From here to 12:13 the book is in Hebrew again; Aramaic ran from 2:4 to 7:28.
b: Daniel 1:1-2:4a is Hebrew, 2:4b-7:28 is Aramaic, and 8:1-12:13 is Hebrew again. Nobody knows why. Proposals include: the Aramaic chapters were first for a wider, Aramaic-speaking audience while the visions of 8-12 were for the learned who read Hebrew (the maskilim of 11:33; 12:3); the Aramaic frame is a deliberate chiasm in 2-7 and 8-12 stands outside it (Collins); the book grew in stages and each stage kept its own language; or the Aramaic chapters were translated or composed from a different source. The line between the languages does not match the line between stories and visions, since chapter 7 is a vision in Aramaic. The Qumran copies 4QDan-a (4Q112) and 4QDan-b (4Q113) preserve this Hebrew verse in part (words in brackets in the transcription are the editors' restorations, not the scroll's). 4QDan-a also has the word 'was revealed' (nigla) visible, with 'a word' before it restored by the editors, as in 10:1; 4QDan-b has no such word (see the variant).

p: A city east of Babylon that later became a Persian royal city; Daniel is there in the vision only, or in person.
b: Susa (Shushan) was the old capital of Elam, east of the Tigris. The Persians made it one of their royal cities, and the books of Esther and Nehemiah (Nehemiah 1:1) set court scenes in 'the fortress at Susa'. In 550 BC, the date of the vision, Susa was not yet the Persian capital it later became, so a reader who dates the book to the sixth century sees Daniel carried in the vision to a place that would soon matter; a reader who dates it later sees the author placing the vision in the Persian heartland to match the ram (8:20). The Hebrew can be read as Daniel being at Susa 'in the vision' only, which most commentators prefer, since Daniel's home is Babylon.

p: A watercourse at Susa, known from Assyrian records; the Hebrew word 'ubal' means a stream or canal.
b: The Ulai is the Eulaeus of Greek writers, a river or canal at Susa. Assyrian records mention a battle at the Ulai in the seventh century BC. The word for 'canal' here is the rare Hebrew 'ubal' (8:2, 3, 6), while 8:16 has 'ben Ulai', literally 'between Ulai', which the Plain takes as 'from the middle of the Ulai' (some say 'between the banks'). Theodotion transliterates 'Ubal' and Old Greek (Swete's Chigi text) reads 'the gate of Elam' in 8:2. Daniel sees visions by water elsewhere, at the Tigris (10:4); compare Ezekiel by the Chebar canal (Ezekiel 1:1).

a: I raised my eyes and saw one ram
p: The angel explains both animals himself (8:20-21), so the reading of the beasts is fixed by the text.
b: Unlike the beasts of chapter 7, whose meaning is argued over, these two are named at once: the ram is Media and Persia, the he-goat is Greece (8:20-21). The taller horn that comes up last (8:3) is Persia, the younger partner who became the stronger. The ram's pushes in three directions (8:4) stand for Persian conquests. Chapter 8 matters for the debate over the four kingdoms of chapters 2 and 7, because it joins Media and Persia as one animal with two horns (see the note at 8:20). Variant: 4QDan-b (where 'great' is visible and 'one' restored) and the Old Greek (Swete's Chigi text) say 'one great ram'.

a: a he-goat came from the west over the face of the whole earth
p: The goat that seems to fly is the Greek conquest of Persia, 334-331 BC.
b: On the usual reading, the goat is Alexander the Great, who crossed from Macedonia into Asia in 334 BC and won at the Granicus (334), at Issus (333) and at Gaugamela (331). By 330 BC the Persian capitals had fallen. 'Not touching the ground' pictures speed: in eleven years Alexander took the Persian empire from Greece to India. Daniel 7:6 gives the leopard four wings for the same reason. The two horns broken in 8:7 are the kings of Media and Persia (8:20) overthrown together. Jewish and Christian readers have read the goat as Greece since early times; Josephus tells that Alexander was shown Daniel's book at Jerusalem (Antiquities 11.8.5), a story whose historical basis is disputed.

p: Alexander died at Babylon in 323 BC, and his generals split his empire; four kingdoms were left by 301 BC.
b: 1 Maccabees 1:5-9 tells the same story: Alexander fell ill and died, and his officers 'put on crowns' and divided the empire. After years of war, the battle of Ipsus in 301 BC left four main kingdoms: Cassander in Macedonia, Lysimachus in Thrace and western Asia Minor, Seleucus in Syria, Mesopotamia and the east, and Ptolemy in Egypt. The text says they would come 'from that nation' (8:22), meaning Greeks, 'but without his strength'. The little horn of 8:9 comes from one of these four, the Seleucid line. Daniel 11:4 repeats the breakup, 'toward the four winds of the heavens'.

p: Antiochus IV for most scholars; Rome, the Antichrist or both for others.
b: The Hebrew says the horn 'comes out of one of these' four, and the text goes on to describe a king (8:23-25). Antiochene: the critical majority, and many conservative scholars including Calvin on Daniel 8, read Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175-164 BC): he campaigned south against Egypt, east into Persia and Armenia, and took the Beautiful Land (Judea). Jewish tradition: Rashi, read on Sefaria, takes the horn to be the kingdom of Titus, Rome. Antiochus as a type: Jerome, who knew Porphyry's reading, says Antiochus is a type of the Antichrist; dispensational writers (Walvoord) see a double fulfillment, Antiochus now and the Antichrist later. Rome: the Adventist and older historicist readings see pagan and then papal Rome (compare the little horn of 7:8, 24-25). Whether chapter 8's horn is the same figure as chapter 7's is itself debated.

p: Hebrew 'ha-tsevi', 'the beauty' or 'the glorious one', a name for the land of Israel.
b: The Hebrew just says 'the tsevi', 'the beauty', and the Plain follows Daniel 11:16, 41 and 45 and the 'beautiful land' of Jeremiah 3:19 and Ezekiel 20:6, 15, where the same word describes the land. A few interpreters take 'the beauty' as the temple or Zion, or as an adjective for 'glory' in general. The three compass points (south, east, Beautiful Land) match Antiochus' campaigns in Egypt (170-168 BC), in the east (165-164 BC) and in Judea.

t: Stars and the army of the sky
p: God's people or the angels: the horn attacks heaven itself.
b: 'The army of the heavens' is the host of stars, which Israel's neighbors worshiped and Israel's writers sometimes made into God's angelic army (Judges 5:20; 2 Kings 17:16). The horn throws some of them to the ground. Most take this as the persecution of the Jewish people, the faithful called stars who will shine in 12:3 (so Collins and others); many ancient readers take it as an attack on angels or on the angelic patron powers (compare Isaiah 14:12-13 and the fallen stars of 1 Enoch's Animal Apocalypse). 2 Maccabees 9:10 says that the dying Antiochus 'had fancied he could reach up and touch the stars of heaven', which hints the Jewish memory read the horn that way.

p: God himself, an angelic commander, or the high priest: each has defenders.
b: 'Prince (sar) of the army (tsava)' echoes 'the commander of the LORD's army' who meets Joshua (Joshua 5:14). Views: God (so the usual reading, since 8:25 speaks of a 'prince of princes' and the sanctuary here is 'his'); Michael or another angelic commander (Daniel 10:21; 12:1); the high priest (Onias III, whom the horn's agents removed in 175-171 BC); and the temple, as Rashi reads it on Sefaria. The Christian reading often sees Christ, as in Joshua 5. 'Prince' is the site's rendering of sar throughout Daniel, so the angelic princes of 10:13, 20-21 can be seen to belong together.

p: Hebrew 'ha-tamid', the twice-daily burnt offering the law required.
b: 'Tamid' means 'continual' or 'regular'. The law required two lambs each day, one at dawn and one at dusk (Exodus 29:38-42; Numbers 28:3-8), and the two daily offerings were the heart of the temple's worship. Antiochus' decree of 167 BC 'stopped burnt offerings, sacrifice and drink offering in the sanctuary' (1 Maccabees 1:45), and Josephus (Antiquities 12.7.6) says the temple was left bare for three years and that Daniel had foretold it. In Christian readings that look to Rome, the offering ended with the burning of the temple in AD 70; in dispensational ones it is a future rebuilt temple's offering; in Adventist ones the 'regular' (tamid) is Christ's continual priestly ministry in heaven, which the 'little horn' (papal Rome) supposedly replaced. Daniel uses 'tamid' at 8:11-13, 11:31 and 12:11.

p: The Hebrew grammar of 8:12 is broken; every translation guesses, and the Greek versions read differently.
b: The Hebrew says, word for word, 'an army will be given over the regular offering in rebellion' (the verbs are in a tense that can be past or future). It is unclear who gives the army, over what, or what 'in rebellion' goes with. The next verb, 'it threw down truth', has a feminine subject, which may be the army, the horn or the rebellion. Some read 'army' as the Jewish people or the temple service rather than a military force. Both Greek versions printed by Swete lack the word 'army' and have 'sin was given on the sacrifice' (Theodotion) or 'sins were put on the sacrifice' (Old Greek). The Plain keeps the order of the Hebrew and leaves the subject of 'threw down truth' open.

p: Two angels talk; one asks 'How long?' as the angels do in Zechariah 1:12 and Revelation 6:10.
b: 'Holy one' (qadosh) is a heavenly being, not a human saint. The scene is a conversation in heaven overheard by Daniel, like the angel who asks 'how long' in Zechariah 1:12. The speaker is called palmoni, a rare Hebrew word meaning something like 'a certain one' or 'so-and-so' (from peloni and almoni); the Plain says 'whoever he was'. Both Greek versions leave it as a name (phelmouni). Jewish tradition (Rashi, read on Sefaria) calls the first speaker an angel. For the people of the holy ones see 8:24.

p: A play on the later phrase 'the abomination that desolates' (9:27; 11:31; 12:11).
b: The Hebrew is pesha shomem, 'rebellion that desolates'. The later phrase in 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11 is shiqqutz meshomem or shomem, 'abomination that desolates'. The sound-play seems deliberate, and many scholars (Collins, Hartman and Di Lella) hear in shomem a deliberate twist of ba'al shamem ('lord of heaven'), the Syrian name for the god the Greeks called Olympian Zeus, whose altar Antiochus set up on the temple altar in December 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54; 2 Maccabees 6:2). The Plain gives pesha as 'rebellion' everywhere (8:12-13; 9:24), and shiqqutz as 'abomination'; see the note at 9:27.

p: Is it 2,300 days, 1,150 days (two offerings each), or 2,300 years? Each reading has its own count.
b: 1,150 days: 'evening and morning' names the two daily offerings, so the number counts offerings, not days: 2,300 offerings is 1,150 days, about three years, the span from the altar's defilement in December 167 BC to its rededication on 25 Kislev 164 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54; 4:52-54). Favored by many (Collins, Montgomery). 2,300 days: 'evening-morning' means a full day, as in Genesis 1, so about six years and four months; defenders count from 171 BC (the murder of Onias III) or 170 BC (Antiochus' first attack on Jerusalem) to 164 BC. 2,300 years: the day-year reading, used by William Miller and the Adventists, who start at 457 BC (Artaxerxes' decree, Ezra 7) and end in AD 1844 (see the card on this chapter). Other: a symbolic number (Young). In Swete's print, both the Old Greek (Chigi) and Theodotion read '2,300 days', which shows their translators took the phrase as days; the Göttingen text and Papyrus 967 were not checked, so this is the printed text of Swete only. 4QDan-b has 'two thousand and three' visible, with the word 'hundreds' restored. See the variant.
r: Daniel 8:26; Daniel 9:24-27; Daniel 12:11-12; Genesis 1:5; 1 Maccabees 1:54; 1 Maccabees 4:52-54; Ezra 7:7-9

p: Hebrew 'nitsdaq' occurs only here; it carries the language of righteousness and has a legal ring.
b: The verb comes from tsedeq, 'righteousness', and means 'to be put in the right', 'vindicated', 'set right'. This is the only place the Niphal form is used of a sanctuary. Theodotion's Greek reads 'will be cleansed' (katharisthesetai; also the Old Greek, in Swete's text), the Latin Vulgate 'cleansed', and so the KJV's 'cleansed' (compare Leviticus 16:19, the Day of Atonement's cleansing of the altar). Adventists connect the word to Yom Kippur and the cleansing of the heavenly sanctuary (Hebrews 9:23); others see only the temple's rededication in December 164 BC, still celebrated at Hanukkah.

p: Gabriel (the name's meaning is debated) is the first angel named in the Bible; he returns in 9:21.
b: The meaning of 'Gabriel' (Gavri'el) is debated: 'man (gever) of God' or 'God is my strength' (both widely given). This is the first angelic name in the Bible. The only other angel the Hebrew Bible names is Michael (Daniel 10:13, 21; 12:1); Tobit adds Raphael (Tobit 12:15). In the New Testament Gabriel announces the births of John and Jesus (Luke 1:19, 26). His job here is interpreter: 'help this man understand'. 1 Enoch lists him among the chief angels (1 Enoch 9:1; 40:9).

p: Hebrew 'ben adam', a human being; not the figure of 7:13.
b: Ben adam is the ordinary Hebrew way to say 'a human being', and God calls Ezekiel by it more than ninety times (Ezekiel 2:1). Here the angel uses it to remind Daniel of his weakness before the heavenly messenger. It is not a title, and it is not the Aramaic 'bar enash' ('one like a son of man') of 7:13, though the same words in two languages mean the same thing and some readers link them. Later Christian use of 'the Son of Man' for Jesus draws on Daniel 7:13 and Ezekiel's address together. The Plain keeps 'son of man' so the idiom is visible.

p: Hebrew 'et qetz'; what end is meant depends on the reading.
b: 'Et qetz' recurs at 8:17, 11:35, 11:40 and 12:4, 9, and the related 'the appointed time of the end' at 8:19 and 11:27, 35. Antiochene: the end of the persecution and of the Seleucid king, the point at which the author expects the kingdom of God (so Collins). Futurist: the end of the age, and Christ's return. Mixed: an end that has both a near fulfillment and a far one, a pattern some call 'double fulfillment'. Jerome, who presents the readings of Porphyry and the church side by side, notes that 'the end' can be used of Antiochus as a type of the Antichrist.

a: stands for the kings of Media and Persia
t: Media and Persia as one animal
p: Chapter 8 treats Media and Persia as one empire, which matters for the four-kingdom debate in chapters 2 and 7.
b: The Hebrew just says 'is' (the ram is the kings of Media and Persia). The ram has two horns, one higher and later, and the text names them together as one empire, 'Media and Persia', as in Esther (Esther 1:3, 18-19) and Daniel 6:8, 12, 15 ('the law of the Medes and Persians'). Defenders of the reading Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome use this verse as proof that the second kingdom of chapters 2 and 7 is Medo-Persia. Critical scholars who read Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece (Collins) answer that chapter 8 belongs to a later vision in which the author joins what he elsewhere keeps apart, or that 'Media and Persia' here is a pair of horns on one beast, not one kingdom. The question is argued in full at chapters 2 and 7.

p: Hebrew 'Yavan' (Javan, the Ionians) is the Bible's word for the Greeks.
b: Yavan is Javan, a son of Japheth in Genesis 10:2, and in later Hebrew the Greeks. The Old Greek and Theodotion render it 'the Greeks (Hellenes)'. It occurs in Isaiah 66:19, Ezekiel 27:13, Joel 3:6, Zechariah 9:13 and here, in 10:20 and 11:2. 'The first king' is Alexander, not as the first king of Greece but as the first king of the Greek empire in Asia. A few interpreters read 'first' as 'foremost'.

a: fierce in face and clever at riddles
t: Fierce in face, clever at riddles
p: A hard-faced king who understands 'chidot': riddles, hints or schemes.
b: Az panim is 'strong/hard of face', shameless or fierce, like the nation 'fierce of face' of Deuteronomy 28:50. Chidot are riddles (Judges 14:12-19; Proverbs 1:6; Psalm 78:2), the 'dark sayings' of the wise. Readings: a master of intrigue and diplomacy (Antiochus' double-dealing: 1 Maccabees 1:30; 2 Maccabees 5:24-26); or one who solves hard questions, as Daniel does in 5:12. Theodotion has 'understanding problems' (problemata), the Old Greek 'riddles' (ainigmata) in Swete's text.

a: though not by his own strength
p: Three readings: God allows it, Satan gives it, or other powers lift him.
b: 'Not by his own power' can mean that God, the real ruler of history, has lent him power for a time (so Jewish and most Protestant readers; compare Daniel 4:17); that Satan empowers him, as the dragon gives the beast its power in Revelation 13:2 (a common Christian reading when the horn is the Antichrist); or that Antiochus gained his throne by court intrigue and the help of others, not by inheriting it (historical reading). The phrase also reads as a contrast with the stone 'not by hands' in 2:34 and with the king 'broken without a hand' in 8:25.

a: the people of the holy ones
t: The people of the holy ones
p: Israel as God's holy people, or the angels' people; the same debate recurs in 7:18-27.
b: Am qedoshim is 'a people of holy ones'. It parallels 'mighty ones' (atsumim) in the same verse and means the faithful Jews whom the king persecutes (so most), as in 7:21, 25 where the horn 'wears out the holy ones of the Most High' (Aramaic). Some read the holy ones as angels throughout (so one reading of 7:18, 22, 25, 27); a mixed reading has the Jews as the angels' earthly counterpart (see the Qumran War Scroll, where Israel and the angels fight together). The Plain does not say 'saints' for qedoshim in Daniel, since 'saints' is Revelation's term.

p: God, the highest ruler. It echoes 'king of kings', which Daniel 2:37 gives to Nebuchadnezzar.
b: Sar sarim is a superlative like 'God of gods' or 'Lord of lords' (Deuteronomy 10:17). It most likely means God. Antiochus took the title 'Epiphanes' ('God made visible') and 2 Maccabees 9:12 has the dying king say that 'it is right to submit to God' and 'No one who is mortal should think arrogant thoughts'. The same expression, reversed to 'a prince of the host', stands in 8:11. Some Christian readers (and Adventists) see Christ, who bears the title 'King of kings and Lord of lords' in Revelation 19:16; Jewish readers have seen God.

a: yet he will be broken without a hand
p: Echoes the stone 'not by hands' in 2:34, 45 and fits Antiochus' sudden death in 164 BC.
b: Be'efes yad means 'with no hand', that is, no human hand: not killed in battle but struck down. The Aramaic of 2:34 and 2:45 says the stone was cut 'not by hands', and the same idea recurs. Antiochus IV died of a sickness in 164 BC while campaigning in the east; 1 Maccabees 6:8-16 describes his grief and death, 2 Maccabees 9 a painful disease, and Polybius (31.9) also reports his death as a divine punishment for trying to rob a temple. Futurist readings apply the line to the Antichrist's destruction by Christ's return (2 Thessalonians 2:8).

p: Hebrew 'satam' (stop up); 12:4 adds 'seal' (chatam). Revelation reverses the order.
b: 'Close up' (satom) is a different verb from 'seal' (chatom), which is used in 9:24 and 12:4, 9, but they work together in 12:4. The command means to keep the vision secret for later. Traditional view: Daniel is told to keep it sealed until the time it concerns (the end of the age, or the coming of Christ, or the church age). Critical view: sealing is a literary convention of apocalypses that claim an ancient author, the mark that a book written in 165 BC says it was written in the sixth century. By contrast, Revelation 22:10 tells John, 'Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, because the time is near.' Compare Isaiah 8:16.

a: went back to the king's work
p: Daniel is still in royal service; the 'king' is Belshazzar on the sixth-century reading.
b: The Hebrew melekhet hamelekh, 'the king's work/business', suggests Daniel kept an official post (compare 2:48-49; 6:2). On the sixth-century reading the king is Belshazzar; Daniel's role was an administrator at court. The verse also contrasts two kinds of understanding: the mighty vision leaves him sick, and 'no one explains it' (or 'no one understood it'): the Hebrew ein mevin can mean both. The Old Greek says 'no one was making it clear'. His distress closes the vision as 7:28 closed chapter 7.

a: In the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus, a descendant of the Medes
p: A king who appears only in Daniel; the views are argued in full at 5:31.
b: Daniel names 'Darius the Mede' at 5:31, 6:1, 9:1 and 11:1. No Babylonian record names him. Views: Gubaru, the governor whom the Nabonidus Chronicle says Cyrus's general appointed in Babylon (Whitcomb and others); Cyrus himself, 'Darius' being a throne title (Wiseman reads 6:28 'Darius, even the reign of Cyrus'); a confused memory of Darius I (522-486 BC), the critical view (Collins), supported by 9:1 calling him 'son of Ahasuerus' (Xerxes, the Ahasuerus of Esther, was Darius I's son, not his father). 'Was made king' is a passive form, which defenders read as meaning someone else installed him. The Old Greek has 'son of Xerxes', Theodotion transliterates 'Ahasuerus'. The date is about 539-538 BC. The fuller discussion is the note at 5:31.

p: 'Sefarim', books: Daniel treats Jeremiah's prophecy as a book he can study.
b: The Hebrew sefarim means 'books' or 'scrolls'. Daniel studies the writings of 'Jeremiah the prophet' with other books, which is one of the earliest hints of a collection of sacred writings. Traditional view: a collection of the prophets existed by about 538 BC; Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (Jeremiah 29) and his oracle in Jeremiah 25 were in circulation. Critical view: the author, working about 165 BC, imagines a Daniel who studies 'the books' because by his time a collection of the prophets existed (compare the grandson's preface to Sirach). Either way, the prayer that follows is the earliest example of one scripture reinterpreted to answer a prayer: Jeremiah's seventy years become the seventy sevens of 9:24.

p: The prophecy of Jeremiah 25:11-12 and 29:10, counted several ways; the site's topic has the details.
b: Jeremiah says Babylon will rule 'seventy years' (Jeremiah 25:11-12) and that when the seventy years are over the LORD will bring the exiles home (Jeremiah 29:10: "When seventy years for Babylon are over, I will turn my attention to you."). The Chronicler explains the seventy years by the law of the land's rest: "until the land had made up for its Sabbaths" (2 Chronicles 36:21), looking back at Leviticus 26:34-35, 43. Counts: from 605 BC (the first deportation, Jeremiah 25:1) to Cyrus's decree in 538, about 67 years; from 586 BC to the temple's dedication in 516, almost exactly 70 (Zechariah 1:12 speaks of 'these seventy years' in 519; Zechariah 7:5 in 518); or a round number. Daniel, about 539/538 BC, thinks the end is near. See the topic on the Seventy Years.
r: Jeremiah 25:11-12; Jeremiah 29:10; 2 Chronicles 36:21; Leviticus 26:34-35; Zechariah 1:12; Ezra 1:1

p: The signs of grief and repentance in the Bible: no food, rough cloth, and ashes.
b: Fasting, sackcloth (a coarse cloth of goat hair) and ashes were the usual signs of mourning and repentance: Nineveh in Jonah 3:5-8, Mordecai in Esther 4:1-3, the community in Nehemiah 9:1. Daniel's prayer comes in the first year of Darius; a second, longer mourning, with a partial fast, comes in 10:2-3. Theodotion's Greek leaves out 'ashes' in Swete's text. The practice answers the covenant's terms: the confession of Leviticus 26:40-42 expects the people to 'confess their guilt' and humble themselves.

p: A prayer of confession like Ezra's and Nehemiah's; only here does Daniel use the name YHWH.
b: Chapter 9's prayer belongs with the 'penitential prayers' of Ezra 9:6-15, Nehemiah 1:5-11, Nehemiah 9:5-37, Baruch 1:15-3:8 (Baruch is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox churches) and the Prayer of Azariah in the Greek Daniel. Qumran has a communal confession in the same style (4Q393). Baruch 1:15-2:19 borrows from Daniel 9 closely. Two features set Daniel 9 apart. The divine name YHWH, 'the LORD', occurs in Daniel only in this chapter (9:2, 4, 8, 10, 13, 14, 20); elsewhere the book says 'God', 'the God of the heavens' and 'the Most High'. And the prayer's style is Deuteronomic, not apocalyptic. Some (Montgomery, Collins) think it was an existing liturgical prayer fitted to the chapter; others (Goldingay) see it as the chapter's heart and original.

a: who keeps the covenant and loyal love
p: The old formula of Deuteronomy 7:9 and Nehemiah 1:5, with the suffixes dropped.
b: Deuteronomy 7:9 says God "keeps his covenant and his loyal love for a thousand generations with those who love him and keep his commands" (Deuteronomy 7:9). Nehemiah's prayer has "the great and fearsome God, who keeps his covenant and his loyal love with those who love him and keep his commands" (Nehemiah 1:5). Daniel has the Hebrew words without 'his': 'the covenant and the loyal love'. The Plain keeps the same 'loyal love' for hesed everywhere. The opening praise sets up the rest of the prayer: God is faithful, so the failure is the people's.

a: We have sinned and gone wrong
t: We have sinned, we have gone wrong
p: Solomon's temple prayer has the same three verbs; Daniel adds 'rebelled' and 'turned away'.
b: Solomon prays that exiles will say, "We have sinned. We have gone wrong. We have done evil" (1 Kings 8:47). Psalm 106:6 uses the same three verbs. Daniel's five verbs (sinned, gone wrong, acted wickedly, rebelled, turned away) pile up the words for sin. The Plain uses 'sin' for chet, 'guilt' for avon, and 'rebellion' for pesha (9:24), as in 1 Kings 8:50. In the Hebrew, 'acted wickedly' has a Ketiv/Qere note in the manuscript tradition: the written form has an extra 'and' (ve-hirsha'nu) and the read form has hirsha'nu. The Plain follows the read form; the difference is only the conjunction.

t: God is right, we are ashamed
p: The prayer 'justifies God': he is in the right, so the exile is deserved.
b: 'Righteousness belongs to you ... but shame of face to us' is the language of a courtroom in which the guilty party agrees with the judge. The Levites say it too: "Yet you are in the right in all that has come on us" (Nehemiah 9:33). The scope of the confession is wide: Judah and Jerusalem, 'all Israel', near and far, even in the lands of exile. This is not only the exiles' guilt; it is the whole people's, over many generations. The Plain's 'the people of the land' (9:6) is am ha-arets, the ordinary landholders.

t: The curse and the oath of the law
p: Deuteronomy 27-30 and Leviticus 26: the covenant's own list of what disobedience would bring.
b: 'The curse (alah) and the oath (shevua)' point to the covenant ceremonies and sanctions in the law of Moses: the curses of Deuteronomy 28:15-68, the 'oath and curse' of Deuteronomy 29:12, 19-20, and Leviticus 26:14-39. Verses 9:11-13 say the whole disaster was written ahead of time, and 'poured out' on the people as the law promised. The prayer's argument is that the exile is not a mistake or a sign of God's weakness but his word being kept, which is also the reason for hope: the same law promises a return when the people confess (Leviticus 26:40-45; Deuteronomy 30:1-5). The verb 'poured out' is used again of the final decree in 9:27.

p: Hebrew 'shaqad', 'to be awake and watching', the verb of Jeremiah's almond branch.
b: Shaqad means to be awake, alert and watching. In Jeremiah 1:11-12 the LORD shows Jeremiah an almond branch (shaqed) and says he is 'watching over' his word to carry it out; Jeremiah 31:28 and 44:27 use the same verb for watching over a nation for harm or for good. Daniel, who has just read Jeremiah (9:2), uses the verb to say that the disaster was not an accident: the LORD stayed awake over it until it came. The same point stands in 9:12, where he has carried out the word he spoke. The Plain translates the verb the same way in each place.

p: The prayer turns from guilt to the old rescue: God made himself a name once, so he can again.
b: 'With a strong hand' and 'made a name for yourself' recall the exodus (Exodus 13:9; 32:11; Nehemiah 9:10; Jeremiah 32:20; Isaiah 63:12). The petition pattern is typical: confess, recall God's great acts, ask him to act again for the sake of his name (9:19). God's reputation is the reason he should act, not the people's worth (9:18). Compare Moses pleading in Exodus 32:11-14 and Numbers 14:13-19.

p: The prayer's words are woven from Psalm 79, Lamentations, Nehemiah and Deuteronomy.
b: 'A disgrace to all who live around us' echoes Psalm 79:4, where the people are a scorn to their neighbors, and the whole of Psalm 79, which also asks God to turn from anger, to forgive for the sake of his name, and not to let the nations ask, 'Where is their God?' (Psalm 79:8-10). 'Your city, your holy mountain' and the sanctuary 'which lies desolate' (9:17) recall Lamentations 5:18. Such borrowing is typical of Second Temple prayer; the author weaves the old language into a new prayer. The Qumran copy 4QDan-e (4Q116) preserves parts of 9:12-17 and shows no difference in meaning from the Masoretic Text in the words that are visible (it writes the fuller spellings, for example 'lo' with a waw); in 9:13 the transcription places the restored name 'YHWH' after 'your truth', so the scroll's word order or wording at that point cannot be judged.

p: Wording from the priestly blessing and the Psalms: God looking on his people with favor.
b: "May the LORD make his face shine toward you and be gracious to you" (Numbers 6:25) is the priestly blessing; the Psalms turn it into a prayer (Psalm 31:16; 80:3, 7, 19). Daniel asks the blessing for a sanctuary, not a person: the temple lies in ruins, and the shine of God's face is what would make it a temple again. Compare the pleas of Ezra and Nehemiah for God's favor on the rebuilding. Theodotion's Greek has 'cause your face to appear' (epiphanon).

a: the city over which your name is called
p: Hebrew 'your name is called over it': God's ownership, and so his honor at stake.
b: To have a name 'called over' something means to claim it as one's own: a conqueror's name is called over a city he takes (2 Samuel 12:28), and God's name is called over Israel (Jeremiah 14:9; 15:16), the temple (1 Kings 8:43) and Jerusalem (here and 9:19; Jeremiah 25:29). Daniel's argument is that if Jerusalem stays in ruins, God's own name is dishonored (9:19). The next clause, 'not because of our righteous deeds', echoes Moses' warning in Deuteronomy 9:4-6 that Israel does not receive the land for its righteousness.

a: my sin and the sin of my people Israel
p: Daniel counts himself a sinner, though the stories of chapters 1-6 show him blameless.
b: Daniel never says in the stories that he sinned; in this prayer he says 'we' from the start and now 'my sin and the sin of my people'. Like Ezra, who says 'my God, I am ashamed' (Ezra 9:6), and Nehemiah, "I and my father's family have sinned" (Nehemiah 1:6), he stands with the people instead of apart from them. The pattern is intercession by one who identifies with the guilty. 'The holy mountain of my God' is Zion, the place the whole prayer is about.

p: The Hebrew 'mu'af bi'af' is uncertain: 'in swift flight' or 'wearied with weariness'.
b: The two words come from a root that can mean 'fly' (uf) or 'be weary' (ya'af), so the phrase is read two ways: 'caused to fly swiftly' (KJV; Theodotion has 'flying' and the Old Greek 'carried quickly', Swete) or 'in extreme weariness', a weary angel coming a long way. The Plain takes the first, since it matches Gabriel's speed in 9:23 ('a word went out, and I have come'). Angels with wings appear in Isaiah 6:2 and Ezekiel 1:6, though Daniel does not say Gabriel has them.

t: The hour of the evening offering
p: About mid-afternoon; Daniel keeps the temple's hour though the temple lies in ruins.
b: Minchat erev, 'the evening grain offering' (Ezra 9:4-5, translated the same way), was offered in mid-afternoon (the 'ninth hour', Acts 3:1). The temple was in ruins in Daniel's day (traditional view), so no offering was made; yet Daniel prays at the hour, as he does three times a day (Daniel 6:10) and as Psalm 141:2 asks ('may the lifting of my hands be like the evening offering'). On the Maccabean reading the temple was functioning when the chapter was composed, but the detail still evokes prayer replacing sacrifice. The same word is used in 9:27 (minchah), where the offerings are stopped.

p: The same phrase, 'the going out of a word', starts the count in 9:25.
b: Gabriel says a word 'went out' when Daniel began to plead (9:23). Verse 9:25 starts the seventy sevens 'from the time a word goes out' (motsa davar) to restore Jerusalem. Some interpreters take both to be the same word, a heavenly decree that goes out now (so the seventy sevens start about 539/538 BC, or with Jeremiah's older word renewed); others read the word of 9:25 as a later human decree, since the verse speaks of a word 'to restore and rebuild Jerusalem'. A starting point in 9:23 would also put the count in Daniel's own lifetime, which is not the usual reading of the Christian and dispensational views, who start with a king's decree (see 9:25).

p: Hebrew 'chamudot', precious things; Daniel is called this three times (9:23; 10:11, 19).
b: Chamudot means 'desirable things', treasures; used of Daniel it is 'one who is greatly desired/loved'. Gabriel says it here and the man in linen repeats it in 10:11 and 10:19. The same word describes the 'choice food' (10:3) Daniel gives up, and 'the desire of women' in 11:37. The Plain keeps 'highly treasured' each time it is said of Daniel. Jewish tradition ties it to Daniel's moral worth; Christian readers sometimes tie it to the elect.

p: 'The vision' (mar'eh) is the word for the evening-and-morning vision of 8:26.
b: Gabriel in 9:21 is 'the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the start'; he is the interpreter of chapter 8, who was told 'help this man understand' (8:16). The word mar'eh for 'the vision' in 9:23 is the word used in 8:26 for 'the vision of the evenings and mornings', not the chazon used elsewhere in chapter 8. So several readers (Adventist writers above all, but also others) take 9:24-27 as the missing explanation of the part of chapter 8 that Daniel could not understand (8:27), namely the 2,300 evenings and mornings. Others read 9:23 as simply 'the vision' of Jeremiah's seventy years. See the note at 8:14 and the Adventist card on chapter 8.

p: Hebrew 'shavu'im', sevens: most readers take them as periods of seven years.
b: The KJV's 'weeks' is a poor guide. Shavu'a means 'a seven', usually seven days (Genesis 29:27-28; Daniel 10:2-3 adds 'of days' to say weeks of ordinary days). Here the plural is the unusual masculine shavu'im, and the Hebrew does not say what is counted. Reasons for years: Jeremiah's seventy years (9:2) set the question; the land's sabbatical years (Leviticus 25:1-7) come in sevens; the penalty 'seven times more' (Leviticus 26:18-28). 70 x 7 = 490. Jewish usage later speaks of a 'week of years'. A few ancient and modern readers keep the sevens symbolic, a perfect number rather than an exact count (Young, Kline). The Plain says 'sevens'.

p: Hebrew 'nechtak' is a rare word, 'cut' or 'decided'; it matters to one Adventist argument.
b: Nechtak occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible. It comes from chatak, 'to cut', and later Hebrew and Aramaic use it for 'decide, determine'. Greek: the Old Greek says the sevens 'were judged', Theodotion 'were cut short' (Swete's text); the Vulgate says 'abbreviatae sunt' ('were shortened'). Seventh-day Adventists read 'cut off': the seventy sevens are cut off from the longer period of 2,300 days in 8:14. Most other readers hold that 'decreed' is the sense, and that nothing is cut from anything. 'Your people and your holy city' means Daniel's people (the Jews) and Jerusalem; dispensational writers stress that it does not say the church.

a: to end the rebellion, to finish sin, to make atonement for guilt
p: Six things the seventy sevens are to accomplish; each reading takes them differently.
b: The six goals are: end the rebellion, finish sin, make atonement for guilt, bring in lasting righteousness, seal up vision and prophet, anoint a most holy place. Antiochene: the end of exile's guilt and the persecution; the temple restored and cleansed in 164 BC. Jewish (Rashi, on Sefaria): Israel's sins are finished and atoned for by exile and the destruction, in a count reaching to the second destruction. Christian messianic: fulfilled in Christ's death and resurrection (Hebrews 9:26; 10:12-14; Romans 3:21-26; 1 Peter 2:24), the church and the sealing of prophecy in Christ. Dispensational: the six goals include the repentance of Israel and the kingdom, so they await the second coming (Walvoord). The grammar groups them: three about sin, three about righteousness and revelation.

a: to anoint a holy of holies
t: Anoint a holy of holies: a place, an altar or a person?
p: Hebrew 'qodesh qodashim' can name the temple's holiest room, the altar, or a person.
b: The Plain says 'a holy of holies' and keeps the question open, because the Hebrew idiom (literally 'a holy place of holy places') does not say which is meant. Qodesh qodashim is the temple's innermost room in Exodus 26:33-34, but it also names the altar (Exodus 29:37), the priestly gifts, and the priest himself (1 Chronicles 23:13, said of Aaron). Altar or temple: rededicated by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:36-59), the usual critical reading. A person: Jesus, anointed with the Spirit (Luke 4:18; Acts 10:38); the Vulgate's 'sanctus sanctorum' lets a Latin reader take it that way. A heavenly sanctuary: Hebrews 9:11-12, 24 (Adventists tie it to the cleansing of 8:14). A future temple: dispensational readers see the temple of Ezekiel 40-48 in the age to come. Jewish tradition: the Second Temple (Rashi). Theodotion has 'anoint a holy of holies'; the Old Greek has 'gladden a holy of holies', a different verb scholars cannot explain with certainty.
r: Exodus 26:33-34; Exodus 29:37; 1 Chronicles 23:13; 1 Maccabees 4:36-59; Hebrews 9:11-12; Luke 4:18

a: from the time a word goes out to restore and rebuild Jerusalem
p: Five starting points produce five different ends; the topic page sets them side by side.
b: 586 BC (Jeremiah's word, Jeremiah 30:18; 31:38): 49 years to Cyrus in 538 fits 'seven sevens' well; the rest of the count is then schematic (Antiochene readings). 538 BC (Cyrus, Isaiah 44:28; Ezra 1:1-4). 520 BC (Darius, Ezra 6:1-12). 458/457 BC (Artaxerxes I in his seventh year, Ezra 7:7-26): used by Adventists, and by many Christian interpreters for a count to Jesus' baptism (AD 26-27) or his death. 445/444 BC (Artaxerxes in his twentieth year, Nehemiah 2:1-8): Julius Africanus (reported by Eusebius), Anderson (360-day years ending at the triumphal entry in AD 32), Hoehner (AD 33). A rabbinic caution cuts the other way: 'May the bones of those who calculate the end rot' (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 97b). Rashi counts 70 years of exile and 420 of the Second Temple; Seder Olam Rabbah 28 gives 70 years for the destruction and 420 for the Second Temple, as read on Sefaria. Ibn Ezra, on Sefaria, counts the seven sevens to the coming of Nehemiah and the sixty-two as the years of the Second Temple. The Hebrew verb in the Plain is 'restore' (lehashiv), which does not by itself mean a return of people.
r: Jeremiah 30:18; Isaiah 44:28; Ezra 1:1-4; Ezra 6:1-12; Ezra 7:7-26; Nehemiah 2:1-8

p: Hebrew 'mashiach nagid': not 'the Messiah' (no article, no capital); the word could name a king or priest.
b: Mashiach means 'anointed', and in the Hebrew Bible usually names a present king or high priest (1 Samuel 24:6; Leviticus 4:3). With no article here, it is 'an anointed one'. Nagid is 'ruler', as elsewhere on the site, not 'prince' (the KJV). Identifications: Cyrus, called the LORD's anointed in Isaiah 45:1 (Rashi, on Sefaria; Seder Olam Rabbah 28 names Cyrus the Persian in its comment on Daniel 11:1-2 and does not discuss the anointed one of 9:25); Jeshua the high priest or Zerubbabel the governor (Zechariah 3-4; 6:11-13); Jesus (Africanus, Eusebius, Jerome records several readings; Calvin); a future Messiah or ruler (dispensational readings, with Jesus' entry into Jerusalem); and in 11QMelchizedek (the Melchizedek scroll) an eschatological figure drawn from this verse. The word 'ruler' next to 'anointed' suggests a king.

a: seven sevens, and sixty-two sevens it will be restored and built again
p: The Leningrad Codex puts the main pause after 'seven sevens'; the Plain's punctuation leaves both divisions possible.
b: In the Leningrad Codex the accent atnach (the main pause of the verse) stands on the word 'seven' (shiv'ah). So the Masoretic reading is: 'until an anointed one, a ruler: seven sevens. And for sixty-two sevens it will be restored and built.' The anointed one is then reached after 49 years, and the sixty-two sevens (434 years) describe the city's time of being rebuilt. Theodotion (in Swete's printing) and the Latin Vulgate put the numbers together, 'seven sevens and sixty-two sevens' before the verb, so that the anointed one arrives after 69 sevens (the Christian count to Jesus). The Old Greek has neither count in this verse. The accents were fixed centuries after Daniel; they record a Jewish reading, and the Greek and Latin record an earlier or different one. The Hebrew has no verb between the numbers, so both readings are possible, and the Plain does not choose: it puts a colon after 'a ruler', a comma after 'seven sevens' and no full stop before the sixty-two, so an English reader can attach 'sixty-two sevens' to either side. See the variant.

p: Hebrew 'rechov' (an open square) and 'charuts' (a trench or moat).
b: Rechov is a broad open space, a plaza or city square (Nehemiah 8:1, 3). Charuts is a cut or trench: a moat or ditch (Joel 3:14 uses it for 'decision'; Isaiah 28:27 for a threshing sledge). Theodotion's Greek reads 'street and wall' and the Vulgate 'street and walls'. The point is a city rebuilt with its squares and defenses, 'in the distress of the times'. For the Nehemiah starting point (445 BC) the distress is the opposition recorded in Nehemiah 4 and 6; for the Antiochene reading it is the continuing troubles of the Persian and Greek period.

a: an anointed one will be cut off
t: The anointed one who is cut off
p: Onias III, Jesus, Agrippa, and others: the identification divides every reading.
b: 'Cut off' (yikkaret) is a word for being killed or removed. Views: Onias III, the high priest murdered in 171 BC (2 Maccabees 4:33-38; Collins and most critical scholars); Jesus, crucified (Africanus, Eusebius, Augustine, Calvin; Young; Baldwin; also the dispensational reading, who place his death after the sixty-ninth seven); Agrippa, king of Judea, in Rashi's reading, read on Sefaria; or an unnamed leader. The word 'cut off' is not the one in Isaiah 53:8, but Christians link the passages. Josephus (Antiquities 10.11.7) tells that Daniel foretold the Roman desolation, though he does not discuss this verse.

a: there will be none for him
t: Nothing for him, or no one?
p: Hebrew 've-ein lo', 'and not to him', leaves out what he lacks: a helper, an heir, a defense, or a reward.
b: The Hebrew means literally 'and there is nothing/no one to him'. Readings: he has nothing, a loss with no object stated (the Plain's 'none'); no one will be left for him (no heir, no helper); 'not for himself', the sense of the KJV, which Christians read as a death for others; or 'no judgment/no fault in him' (Theodotion's Greek in Swete: 'there is no judgment in him'). The Old Greek says 'and will not be', and Jerome's Latin adds a clause about a people who will deny him. The Plain keeps the bare phrase because the grammar does not say.

a: The people of a ruler who is coming
t: The people of the coming ruler
p: Roman soldiers under Titus in AD 70, Antiochus' forces in 167 BC, or a future empire's people.
b: The Hebrew says 'the people of a ruler who is coming' will destroy the city and the holy place. Roman view: Titus and his legions, AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 6; Rashi, on Sefaria; Jerome; most Christian interpreters, including Young and Baldwin). Antiochene view: the forces of Antiochus, who struck Jerusalem in 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:29-32). Dispensational view: the 'people' are the Romans of AD 70, but the 'ruler who is coming' is the future Antichrist from a revived Roman empire (Walvoord). The connection of the ruler to 'the he' in 9:27 is the crux: if 'he' is this ruler, the covenant-maker is the coming prince.

a: Its end will come in the flood
p: The flood is a picture of invasion, as in Isaiah 8:7-8 and Nahum 1:8.
b: Shetef is an overflowing flood, a standard picture of an army sweeping over a land (Isaiah 8:7-8; Nahum 1:8; Daniel 11:10, 22, 26, 40). No literal flood is meant. 'His end' or 'its end' is not clear in Hebrew: the ending -o can be 'his' or 'its', and might refer to the ruler, the city or the holy place; Theodotion has a plural, 'they will be cut off in a flood'. The Plain says 'its end'. The Hebrew has 'the flood' with the article.

a: He will make a covenant strong for the many
p: The subject of this verse decides the reading: the ruler, the anointed one, or Antiochus' ally.
b: The Hebrew has no named subject, and no pronoun at all: 'He' is the translator's forced choice of English pronoun, and the nearest antecedents are 'a ruler who is coming' (9:26) and 'an anointed one' (9:26). Antiochene: a Seleucid king or his agents, and 'the many' are the Jews who joined the Greek ways: "let us make a covenant with the nations around us" (1 Maccabees 1:11); one seven is the last years, 171-164 BC. Messianic: 'he' is the anointed one of 9:26; he confirms God's covenant with the many (Isaiah 53:11-12; Mark 14:24), is 'cut off' in the middle of the seventieth seven, and ends the old sacrifice by his death (Hebrews 10:8-14; Young, Baldwin). Titus: 'he' makes a treaty with Jewish leaders and breaks it (Rashi, on Sefaria). Dispensational: 'he' is the coming ruler of 9:26, the Antichrist, who makes a seven-year treaty with Israel after a gap of the church age and breaks it at the midpoint (Walvoord). Critics, including other premillennial writers, doubt both the gap and the change of subject. 'The many' (rabbim) is a Semitic way to say the whole group concerned, not a part of it; see 12:2 and Isaiah 53:11-12.

a: In the middle of the seven
p: Three and a half years in each reading; what happens then differs.
b: Half of a seven is three and a half years, the length elsewhere given as 'a time, times and half a time' (Daniel 7:25; 12:7) and 1,290 days (12:11). Antiochene: the sacrifice stopped in December 167 BC and was restored in December 164 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54; 4:52-54), about three years, the 'half' of the last seven. Messianic: Jesus' ministry (about three and a half years) ends with the cross, which ends the need for sacrifice; some start the half-seven later at his baptism. Preterist and Jewish (Rashi): the Jewish war against Rome began in AD 66 and the temple fell in AD 70, three and a half years. Dispensational: the midpoint of the future seven-year tribulation (Revelation 11:2-3; 12:6, 14; 13:5).
r: Daniel 7:25; Daniel 12:7; Daniel 12:11; Revelation 11:2-3; Revelation 12:6; Revelation 13:5

p: A pair meaning all temple offerings; Psalm 40 and Hebrews 10 play on it.
b: Zevach u-minchah, 'sacrifice and offering', covers all offerings, animal and grain, as in Psalm 40:6 ('sacrifice and offering you did not desire'), which Hebrews 10:5-8 quotes in its Greek form to say that Christ's body takes the place of the old sacrifices. The Maccabean reading ties the phrase to the edict that stopped "burnt offerings, sacrifice and drink offering in the sanctuary" (1 Maccabees 1:45). The Christian reading takes Hebrews 10:9, where Christ takes away the first order to set up the second, as the fulfillment. For the dispensational view it names a future temple's offerings.

p: Hebrew 'kenaf shiqqutsim': 'wing' is odd; the Greek and Latin read 'on the temple'.
b: Kanaf is 'wing', hence also a corner, edge or projecting part (a robe's hem, the 'wing' of a building). Readings: on the pinnacle or corner of the temple (Matthew 4:5 uses the Greek pterygion, 'little wing', of the temple's pinnacle); 'on the wing', meaning in the train of or borne along by abominations; or a corrupted text. Both Greek versions read 'on the temple (hieron) the abomination of desolations' (Swete), and the Vulgate 'in the temple will be the abomination of desolation'. Matthew 24:15 follows with 'standing in a holy place'. The Plain translates the Hebrew words and leaves the difficulty in the note; the next note says how Matthew 24:15 and Mark 13:14 relate to the phrase.

p: The site's rendering of this phrase, and what it was: Antiochus' altar, a Roman act, or an Antichrist.
b: The Hebrew shiqqutz means a detestable, idolatrous thing; meshomem or shomem means 'making desolate', in a pun on 8:13 ('the rebellion that desolates') and on ba'al shamem. Decision for the whole book: shiqqutz meshomem (11:31; 12:11) is 'the abomination that desolates'; here the plural 'abominations' and the person 'one who makes desolate' are kept as the Hebrew has them. Matthew 24:15 (site Plain: 'the abomination of desolation') and Mark 13:14 quote the Greek rendering (bdelygma tes eremoseos). 1 Maccabees 1:54 says "they built an abomination of desolation on the altar" (1 Maccabees 1:54). Applications: Antiochus' altar to Zeus Olympios, December 167 BC; the Roman standards in AD 70 (Luke 21:20); Caligula's statue plan in AD 40; the Antichrist in a rebuilt temple (2 Thessalonians 2:4).
r: Daniel 8:13; Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11; Mark 13:14; Matthew 24:15; 1 Maccabees 1:54; 2 Thessalonians 2:4

a: until full destruction, the end that was decided
t: A destruction decided and poured out
p: Isaiah's 'end, a settled end' (Isaiah 10:23; 28:22) lies behind the wording.
b: 'Complete destruction and what has been decided' reuses Isaiah's kalah ve-nechratsah: 'an end, a settled end' (Isaiah 10:23; 28:22). In Isaiah the settled end falls on the whole land; in Daniel it falls on the one who desolates. The thought that the desolator will in the end be desolated is the book's answer to its persecutors. Compare the fate of the horn, 'broken without a hand' (8:25), and of the king in 11:45.

a: is poured out over the one who makes desolate
t: The curse poured out, and poured back
p: Claude's theory: the verb 'poured out' ties the end of the desolator to the curse of 9:11.
b: The verb tittakh, 'is poured out', is used in Daniel only twice: of the curse and the oath poured out on Israel (9:11), and of the decreed end poured out on the one who makes desolate (9:27). That the same verb stands in both places is a fact of the text. The suggestion here is Claude's own: that the author means a reversal, in which the wrath that the law's curse poured on Israel in exile is, at the end of the seventy sevens, poured back on the desolator. Online commentary collections read in a search do say that the decreed end falls on the desolator, which is the commentators' ordinary reading of the verse; none of those found drew the link to 9:11. That is a limit of the search (Collins and Goldingay on 9:27 were not read for this), not proof that the idea is unpublished. The idea would tie the prayer's confession (9:4-19) to the answer (9:24-27) on a single image: Israel's guilt is dealt with in the seventy sevens (9:24), so the wrath moves to the oppressor. It does not decide among the readings above. Both Greek versions read 'will be given' here, not 'poured out' (see the variant).

a: In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia
p: About 536 BC, two or three years after the first exiles went home (Ezra 1:1-4); Daniel stays in Babylonia.
b: Cyrus took Babylon in October 539 BC. His first year over Babylon is 538 (Ezra 1:1), so the third is about 536 BC, if the count is from the conquest. Daniel is by then an old man, about 85 on the traditional dating (compare 1:21, 'until the first year of King Cyrus'). The book does not say why he did not go back with the exiles. The chapter links to the earlier visions: the vision of chapter 8 was in Belshazzar's third year, this one in Cyrus's third. Critical readers see the author keeping a tidy chronology for a Persian-period setting; defenders see a real date. The last dated vision of the book opens the long revelation of chapters 10-12.

t: A great war, or hard service?
p: Hebrew 'tsava' can mean war, army, or hard service; the chapter's contents decide.
b: Tsava is 'army' in 8:10-13 (the army of the sky). It can also mean a term of hard service, as in Isaiah 40:2 ('her term of service is over') and Job 7:1. So 'a great war' can also be read 'a great struggle', a long hard time, or 'a great army' (the Old Greek has 'the great host', in Swete's text). Chapters 10-12 tell of a war in heaven (10:13, 20) and wars on earth (chapter 11), which fits 'war'. The Plain says 'a great war'.

p: The Hebrew adds 'days' to mark ordinary weeks, unlike the 'sevens' of chapter 9.
b: Here the Hebrew says shavu'im yamim, 'sevens of days', where chapter 9 says only 'sevens'. Daniel marks the difference on purpose: these are ordinary weeks, twenty-one days. The contrast is one reason many readers take the sevens of 9:24-27 to be years, since the writer could have added 'of days' and did not. The twenty-one days of mourning match the twenty-one days the prince of Persia withstood the angel (10:13).

a: I ate no fine food. No meat or wine came into my mouth
p: Daniel gives up rich food, meat, wine and oil, not all food: the same kind of fast as in chapter 1.
b: This is a partial fast and a time of mourning. 'Fine food' is literally 'bread of desirable things' (the same word as 'highly treasured' in 9:23), so the Plain says 'fine food'. Leaving off oil (for the skin and hair) was a mark of grief (2 Samuel 14:2). Compare Daniel's earlier choice of vegetables and water (1:8-16) and see the topic on Fasting. If the three weeks end on the date in 10:4 (the twenty-fourth), they began about the third or fourth of the first month, so they cover Passover (14 Nisan) and the week of unleavened bread (15-21 Nisan); the text says nothing about a festival, and this is only an observation about the calendar.

p: Hebrew 'Hiddekel', the Tigris, one of the four rivers of Eden.
b: The Hebrew name is Chiddeqel, the Tigris, named in Genesis 2:14. Ezekiel saw visions by the Chebar canal (Ezekiel 1:1) and Daniel saw one by the Ulai (8:2). The Tigris flowed through the heart of Mesopotamia; if Daniel was in Babylon (as 8:27 suggests he was) he was a few days' journey from it. The first month is Nisan (Nehemiah 2:1; Esther 3:7). The Old Greek and Theodotion both render the name as Tigris.

t: Who is the man in linen?
p: Gabriel, another angel, or a glory of the LORD: Jews and Christians have read him all three ways.
b: Linen (baddim) is the dress of angels and priests: the 'man in linen' of Ezekiel 9:2-3 and 11, and the priest's linen on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:4). He appears again above the river in 12:6-7. An angel (the usual reading in Jewish tradition and in much Christian reading): he speaks of 'princes' and of a fight, and says he was sent (10:11). Whether he is Gabriel is not stated. A divine figure: some Christian readers, from early times, saw the preincarnate Christ because Revelation 1:13-16 describes Jesus in almost the same words; Revelation's author clearly draws on this verse. The description is a vision-description more than a name. The Old Greek (in Swete's text) adds 'and light out of his middle'.

p: A place named only here and in Jeremiah 10:9; some think it is a slip for Ophir.
b: Uphaz is not known as a place. The only other Bible mention of 'gold from Uphaz' is Jeremiah 10:9. Ophir (1 Kings 9:28) is the famous gold land, and the two names look much alike in Hebrew (אופז and אופיר), so some scholars take Uphaz as a copying change; others take it as a real, distant source of gold. Theodotion transliterates it ('Ophaz'); the Old Greek in Swete's text has no gold at all. The detail only says that his belt was the finest gold. Rashi, read on Sefaria, says the belt was studded with jewels.

p: Hebrew 'tarshish', a gem (the Plain follows Exodus 28:20) or, in Rashi's reading, the sea.
b: The Hebrew word tarshish names a gem in Exodus 28:20, where the Plain says 'chrysolite' (a yellow-green stone, perhaps what we call topaz or beryl). It is the same stone as in Ezekiel 1:16 (the wheels), Ezekiel 10:9, Ezekiel 28:13 and Song of Songs 5:14. Revelation 21:20 lists 'chrysolite' among the foundation stones. Rashi, read on Sefaria, says the Sages took it as the sea, since Tarshish was across the sea. Either way the picture is a body that shines like a jewel. The Old Greek in Swete's text says 'like the sea' for the mouth (10:6) and misses the stone.

p: Revelation 1:13-15 borrows this picture: lightning face, fire eyes, bronze feet, roaring voice.
b: Revelation 1:14-15 says of Jesus, 'his eyes were like a flame of fire' and 'His feet were like polished bronze', and his voice 'like the roar of many waters'. Daniel 10:6 has eyes like torches of fire, arms and feet like polished bronze, a voice like the sound of a crowd. Ezekiel 1:13-14, 24, 27 supplies the fire, bronze and noise. Revelation merges this figure with the 'one like a son of man' of Daniel 7:13 (compare 'one like a son of man' in Revelation 1:13). Whether that means Daniel's figure was Christ, or John used an angel's description to portray Christ, is debated. Revelation 10:1 also uses the same description for a mighty angel.

a: The men with me did not see it
p: Those with the seer feel the terror but see nothing; Paul's companions have the same experience in Acts 9:7.
b: The same pattern shows in Acts: Paul's companions 'heard the voice, but they saw no one' (Acts 9:7), and 'did see the light, but the voice of the one who spoke to me they did not hear' (Acts 22:9). The vision is for one person; those near him shake without knowing why. It marks the vision as a revelation, not a public event. 'Ran off to hide' recalls the fear before a holy presence (Genesis 3:8-10; Exodus 20:18-19). The men are not named; the Old Greek has them flee 'in haste', Theodotion 'in fear'.

p: Hebrew 'hit'annot', 'to make oneself low': fasting and humbling before God.
b: Hit'annot is the reflexive of 'anah, 'be low, afflict'. It is the verb for the humbling in Leviticus 16:29-31 ('you must humble yourselves', the Day of Atonement fast) and Ezra 8:21. Gabriel's answer ties Daniel's three weeks of fasting (10:2-3) to the hearing of his prayer, from the first day. The phrase 'set your mind' echoes 'I set my face' in 9:3. The Greek of Theodotion has 'be afflicted' (kakothenai), the Old Greek 'be humbled' (Swete).

a: the prince of the kingdom of Persia
p: Angelic powers over the nations: this is the Bible's clearest picture of conflict behind politics.
b: The 'prince of the kingdom of Persia' and 'the prince of Greece' (10:20) are heavenly beings set over nations, with Michael as the prince of Israel (10:21; 12:1). The idea belongs to Deuteronomy 32:8-9, where in the Qumran and Greek reading God divides the nations 'to match the number of the sons of God', and Israel is the LORD's own share; also Sirach 17:17 and Jubilees 15:31-32. Angelic patrons (so most): the unseen side of what happens on earth; Rashi, read on Sefaria, says the prince of Persia asked in heaven that Persia's rule be lengthened so it could keep Israel subject. Human rulers: the Persian king, or the angels as stand-ins for the kings. Demonic powers: many Christian readers (and the 'territorial spirits' idea in some charismatic teaching) see evil powers behind nations (Ephesians 6:12). Daniel does not call them evil; he says only that they opposed him. See the Where Christians differ card.
r: Deuteronomy 32:8-9; Daniel 10:20-21; Daniel 12:1; Psalm 82:1; Sirach 17:17; Jubilees 15:31-32; Ephesians 6:12

p: The same three weeks as Daniel's mourning: the delay and Daniel's fast run side by side.
b: Daniel mourned 'three weeks of days' (10:2), and the angel was held up 'twenty-one days' (10:13). The match suggests that the angel left at the start of the fast ('From the first day...', 10:12) and arrived at the end. It is not said that the fast helped Michael win; the text only places the two in parallel. Prayer on earth and war in heaven run together, as in Revelation 8:3-5 and 12:7-12. Daniel's prayer works, but the answer takes time.

a: Michael, one of the chief princes
t: Michael, one of the chief princes
p: Michael first appears here; Daniel calls him a chief prince, and later (12:1) 'the great prince'.
b: Michael (Mi-kha-el, 'Who is like God?') is named in Daniel 10:13, 21 and 12:1, and then in Jude 9 and Revelation 12:7. Daniel calls him 'one of the chief princes' here, 'your prince' (10:21) and 'the great prince who stands over your people' (12:1). Christian tradition makes him an archangel, a created being; Jehovah's Witnesses identify him with Jesus before and after his earthly life; Adventist writing since Uriah Smith has widely taught the same, though it is not one of the Adventist Fundamental Beliefs. Reformed commentators are divided: Calvin, on Daniel 12:1, says that many understand Michael as Christ and that, if the archangel seems better, the sense still fits, since angels serve under Christ as head. See the card below and the topic on Michael. Qumran's War Scroll gives Michael a leading role in the end-time war.

p: Hebrew 'notarti' can mean 'I was left over', 'I remained', or 'I was detained'; the Greek reverses who was left.
b: Notarti means 'I was left behind/left over' (from yatar). The speaker was kept there, or stayed there, or was no longer needed there. Both Greek versions in Swete's text read 'I left him [Michael] there with the ruler of the kingdom of Persia', so the angel is the one who leaves Michael as a guard. Whether the Greek translators read a different Hebrew or simply smoothed a hard sentence cannot be shown, since the wording differs in more than one letter. Also, the Hebrew says 'kings of Persia' (plural) where the Greek has the singular king or 'kingdom'.
orig: וַאֲנִי נוֹתַרְתִּי שָׁם אֵצֶל מַלְכֵי פָרָס

p: Hebrew 'acharit hayamim': the later part of the days, a time the speaker looks toward.
b: Acharit hayamim is 'the end/latter part of the days'. It is used for the future after some event, in Genesis 49:1, Numbers 24:14, Isaiah 2:2 and Hosea 3:5. The Plain says 'in the last days' where the future end is meant (Genesis 49:1; Numbers 24:14) and 'in the days to come' where the future is nearer (Isaiah 2:2). Here it opens chapter 11, which runs from Persia to the persecution under Antiochus; many Christian readers extend it to the end of the age. See the topic on the Last Days.

p: Like Isaiah's coal and Jeremiah's hand, the touch frees the prophet to speak.
b: Daniel is touched three times (10:10, 16, 18) and each time he is brought a step closer to speaking. The touch on the lips echoes Isaiah 6:7 ('now that this has touched your lips, your guilt goes away') and Jeremiah 1:9; Ezekiel is made mute and then allowed to speak (Ezekiel 3:26-27). The same angel-type appears in Luke 1:19-20, where Gabriel strikes Zechariah silent. Daniel's muteness (10:15) is the response of a seer overwhelmed by what he sees; the touch is a commission to speak with the interpreter.

p: After Persia comes Greece; the heavenly struggle looks ahead to the Greek conquest.
b: The angel will go on fighting the prince of Persia and, when he leaves, the prince of Greece will arrive. This foretells the shift of world power from Persia to Greece described in 8:5-8 and 11:2-4, and matches the earthly sequence: the contest above is the contest below. Chapter 11 goes on to the kings of the north and south (the Seleucids and Ptolemies), whose princes are not named. The Old Greek and Theodotion both read 'prince of the Greeks (Hellenes)'.

p: A heavenly book in which events are written ahead of time.
b: The 'writing (ketav) of truth' is a heavenly record of what will happen, like the 'books' opened at the judgment in 7:10 and the 'book' of 12:1. Compare the book of Exodus 32:32-33 and Psalm 139:16, and the 'heavenly tablets' of 1 Enoch (81:1-2; 103:2) and Jubilees. Traditional view: God's plan for history, which angels carry out. Critical view: a literary device of apocalypse, in which history is already written and the persecution is a stage in a fixed plan (Collins). Rashi, read on Sefaria, explains it as 'the document of the decree'. Compare the 'book of life' topic.

p: 'Your' is plural: Michael is the prince of Daniel's people, Israel.
b: 'Your prince' is plural in Hebrew (sarkhem), so it means 'the prince of you all', of Daniel's people (compare 12:1, 'the great prince who stands over your people'). In Deuteronomy 32:9 Israel is the LORD's own share, and here his heavenly representative is Michael. The Qumran War Scroll gives Michael the same role. The idea that the angels of the nations contend while the people on earth suffer sits behind later Jewish and Christian pictures of Michael as the defender of God's people (Jude 9; Revelation 12:7).
